provisions_triggered.name: Due Process / Law of the Land

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that a preponderance standard violates due process in parental termination proceedings and that the State must support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence.
key_cases.relevance: Is the federal constitutional source of the clear-and-convincing burden Tennessee applies in every termination case.
key_cases.quote: We hold that such a standard adequately conveys to the factfinder the level of subjective certainty about his factual conclusions necessary to satisfy due process.

key_cases.holding: The Tennessee Supreme Court held that the Department need not prove reasonable efforts to reunify as a precondition to termination; the extent of its efforts is instead weighed in the best-interests analysis.
key_cases.relevance: Controls the elements the State must prove in a Tennessee termination case.
key_cases.quote: the extent of DCS's efforts to reunify the family is weighed in the court's best-interest analysis, but proof of reasonable efforts is not a precondition to termination

key_cases.holding: The court held that due process entitles parents to fundamentally fair procedures in termination proceedings, that Tennessee's statutory right to appointed counsel plus mandatory appellate review of every ground and the best-interest finding supply that fairness, and that no collateral ineffective-assistance attack is available.
key_cases.relevance: Sets the procedural due-process framework and appellate review duty for every Tennessee termination case.
key_cases.quote: We hold that parents are constitutionally entitled to fundamentally fair procedures in parental termination proceedings.

key_cases.holding: Resolving a split, the court held that Tenn. Code Ann. sec. 36-1-113(g)(14) imposes a conjunctive obligation to manifest both ability and willingness, so failure to manifest either satisfies the ground's first prong, and reinstated termination.
key_cases.relevance: Defines the elements of one of Tennessee's most frequently used termination grounds.
key_cases.quote: places a conjunctive obligation on a parent or guardian to manifest both an ability and willingness to personally assume legal and physical custody or financial responsibility for the child

key_cases.holding: The court held the statutory definitions of willful failure to support unconstitutional because they created an irrebuttable presumption of abandonment regardless of intent, and ordered the child returned to her father under a gradual transition plan.
key_cases.relevance: States the constitutional predicate - parental unfitness or substantial harm - that underlies every Tennessee termination ground.
key_cases.quote: there must be a showing that the parent is unfit or that substantial harm to the child will result if parental rights are not terminated

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed termination for abandonment by willful failure to visit, holding that abandonment must be willful and cannot be found where a parent's visitation efforts were thwarted, but that this father's failure was willful because the mother never denied him access.
key_cases.relevance: Is the Tennessee Supreme Court source of the willfulness element of abandonment and of the thwarted-visitation answer to it.
key_cases.quote: the abandonment must be willful, and where a parent has been thwarted in visitation efforts, we have refused to find willful abandonment
